references.text: Isaiah describes the people who walk in darkness but see a great light, a direct parallel image to Jesus' claim of being the light of the world that leads out of darkness.
Here the Messiah is described as a light for the nations, who will open the eyes of the blind and lead prisoners out of darkness, which mirrors the function of 'the light of life' in John 8:12.
This psalm verse is a direct parallel to the expression 'I am the light,' where the Lord is referred to as both light and salvation, and as the one who gives security against darkness.
The word is described as a light that shines on the path, an image of divine guidance that prevents one from walking in darkness, just like Jesus' words about following him.
Here God is defined as 'full light' without darkness, and it is emphasized that those who walk in the light have fellowship, which corresponds with the promise not to walk in darkness.
In the new Jerusalem there is no night, for the glory of the Lord is its light, an eschatological fulfillment of the promise to have 'the light of life' and no longer walk in darkness.
